newsitem.title: CONGO: Thousands of Rwandan Hutus hide in Congo forest.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of Rwandan Hutus hide in Congo forest.

text.p: Thousands of frightened Rwandan Hutu refugees are hiding in the eastern jungle of Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of the Congo, field officers from the U.N. refugee agency say.

But aid workers, who are trying to entice the refugees out of the forest, say that like fellow Rwandan Hutus who made a nightmare trek west across much of Africa's third largest nation, many are keen to return home.

"There is still great fear among refugees and getting them over that fear is a big problem," says Joe Brady of the UNHCR agency at the remote and abandoned tin-mining town of Lulingu, 300 km east of regional capital Bukavu by mud road.
"They are desperately anxious to go home."
Relief officials and local authorities estimate around 14,000 Rwandan Hutus are spread out in a vast area of thick primary rainforest around Lulingu.

Unlike tens of thousands of fellow refugees who fled all the way across the then Zaire during Kabila's seven-month civil war against former dictator Mobutu Sese Seko, these refugees remain within 300 kms (200 miles) of their former camps on the borders.

On Monday, about 300 refugees in Lulingu began fleeing when one brought in reports of gun shots outside town. Local villagers said it was the sound of burning bamboo and by Wednesday the refugees had returned.
They fear Kabila's army, which includes many ethnic Tutsis, and retribution for the 1994 genocide of up to a million ethnic Tutsis in Rwanda.
Persistent reports suggest refugees were massacred by Kabila's alliance army and Rwandan Tutsi allies around Shabunda, just north of Lulingu.
But apart from villagers reporting bones, little concrete evidence has emerged to substantiate massacres around Shabunda, where by January around 40,000 refugees had gathered.
"It's at Shabunda they started killing people," Marie Grace, a 15-year-old refugee at Lulingu said, but like others she gave few details.
The UNHCR has repatriated by air over 52,000 refugees emerging from all corners of the former-Zaire over the past weeks. They estimate up to 200,000 are unaccounted for.

Lulingu is practically unreachable by road. Refugees are hiding in even more isolated villages. Villagers and aid workers say the forest also shelters hardline Hutu Interahamwe militia and soldiers of the former Rwandan army -- implicated in the Rwanda genocide -- who could try to obstruct repatriation as in the past.
The UNHCR plans to bring in Buffalo aircraft to a small airstrip to repatriate refugees, 80 at a time, to Rwanda.

The local hospital is caring for 128 refugees, 47 sick or malnourished. Local doctors who were formerly employed by the Sominki mining company which ran the local tin mine have been treating the refugees for free since January.

The clean red brick hospital is an unlikely site in the thick jungle. Built in 1946 by Congo's former colonial rulers, the Belgians, it has 200 beds, a laboratory, and an operating theatre where villagers pay around $1 for surgery. But until aid groups came three weeks ago, medicines were in short supply.
